deed: סלמן ואקסמן ותלמידו הוציאו מהאדמה את האנטיביוטיקה הראשונה נגד שחפת
title: The discovery of streptomycin – the first antibiotic against tuberculosis

trailer.text: Selman Waksman was a researcher of the decomposition of organisms that live in soil, and headed the Institute of Microbiology at Rutgers University until his retirement in 1958.
Selman Waksman received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for the discovery of streptomycin, the first antibiotic effective against tuberculosis.
Sanatoriums were then filled with tuberculosis patients, and very little could be done for them.
Waksman and his colleagues screened more than 10,000 soil microorganisms, and in 1943 his colleague Albert Schatz isolated streptomycin, which proved to be an effective medicine against tuberculosis.
The discovery of streptomycin changed the course of modern medicine.

paragraphs.text: Robert Koch discovered that a bacterium causes tuberculosis, and then the race to find a cure began.
When streptomycin was discovered, tuberculosis was the most resistant and irreversible of the major infectious diseases.
Sanatoriums around the country were filled with tuberculosis patients, and very little could be done for them.
In the years of the Second World War, the tuberculosis bacterium was the worst, because it resisted every antibiotic that was available.

stations.title: From a Jewish village to Rutgers

paragraphs.text: According to the facts page on the Nobel Prize website, the village of Priluka was in the Russian Empire (today Nova Pryluka in Ukraine).
According to Encyclopedia.com, his little sister Miriam died of diphtheria when he was nine years old.
As a youth, Waksman helped organize an armed Jewish youth defense group against oppression.
According to one source, he fled prejudice and poverty and arrived in the United States in 1910.
On 2 November 1910 he landed in Philadelphia, accompanied by his friend Peisi Mitnik.
Waksman studied at Rutgers, and in 1915 completed a bachelor's degree in agricultural science.
According to the archive of Rutgers University Libraries, Selman Abraham Waksman was born in Priluka, Russia, on July 22, 1888.

stations.title: Searching for a cure in the soil

paragraphs.text: In 1932 the American Association against Tuberculosis asked Waksman to investigate reports that the tuberculosis bacterium was rapidly destroyed in soil.
According to Wikipedia, Waksman's research into the decomposition of organisms that live in soil enabled the discovery of streptomycin and other antibiotics.
In 1939 René Dubos, his former student, discovered tyrothricin, and this was among the reasons Waksman began the antibiotics program.
According to Encyclopedia.com, he set up a team that systematically studied thousands of soil fungi and microorganisms.
In 1940, with the help of Boyd Woodruff, Waksman isolated the antibiotic actinomycin.
According to Woodruff, the team quickly discovered four antibiotics, but all of them were toxic to animals.
Waksman and his colleagues screened more than 10,000 soil microorganisms before they isolated streptomycin in 1943.

stations.title: Albert Schatz and the strain from the soil

paragraphs.text: Albert Schatz, the newest doctoral student in the group, arrived and began his research under Waksman.
He was drafted into the army, and after a few months he was released and returned to searching for a useful antibiotic.
According to Woodruff, Schatz isolated a Streptomyces griseus strain from the farm soil of the Rutgers Agriculture School.
On 19 October 1943 Schatz realized that he had a chemical that killed tuberculosis bacteria.
In 1943 Schatz isolated streptomycin from the bacterium, and it proved to be an effective medicine against tuberculosis.
Elizabeth Bugie was the second author of the original paper on streptomycin.
According to Woodruff, Mayo Clinic experts tested the substance and reported that it was not toxic to various animals.
According to Woodruff, streptomycin cured infected guinea pigs, and was the first drug to do so.
Clinical trials showed that streptomycin was effective against a wide range of diseases, most notably tuberculosis.
By 1950 it was used against seventy germs that could not be treated with penicillin.
The Merck company built a factory in Virginia to produce streptomycin, and the drug was marketed worldwide.
When it became clear how important streptomycin was, Merck agreed to transfer its rights to Rutgers University, and the university licensed several companies to manufacture it.
According to San Diego Jewish World, Waksman transferred the exclusive rights to streptomycin to the university where it was discovered.
According to Woodruff, Waksman argued that purified antibiotics were no longer natural products and could therefore be patented, and so it was ruled.
Manufacture of the drug became a $50-million-per-year industry.

stations.title: Nobel, an institute and a generation of drugs

paragraphs.text: According to the Odessa Journal, Waksman was nominated for the Nobel Prize 45 times, and received it only in 1952.
In 1952 he traveled to Sweden to receive the Nobel Prize in Medicine for the discovery of streptomycin.
In the award presentation speech, Arvid Wallgren said that penicillin was discovered largely by chance, whereas streptomycin was developed through the systematic work of a large group of scientists.
According to Encyclopedia.com, the Rutgers foundation assigned most of the royalties from streptomycin and neomycin to the establishment of the Institute of Microbiology.
According to EBSCO, Waksman headed the institute until his retirement in 1958.
The development of streptomycin stimulated scientists around the world to search the microbial world for other antibiotics and medicines.
According to the Odessa Journal, today more than 70% of antibiotics are produced from Actinomycetales.

stations.title: Who discovered it, and what the drug did not solve

paragraphs.text: According to Woodruff, streptomycin treatment often required about half a year, and as a result resistant tuberculosis cells appeared.
It was later found that streptomycin is somewhat toxic to humans, and other antibiotics replaced it.
According to Shaastra, Schatz and Waksman applied for a patent together, and Waksman persuaded Schatz to sign over his royalty rights to the university.
According to Shaastra, Waksman secretly negotiated with the university to receive 20% of the royalties.
According to Shaastra, Schatz felt betrayed and sued both his mentor and the university.
According to the NJ Digital Highway website, Schatz became concerned when Waksman began receiving funds from the foundation, $380,000 according to his claim, and filed a civil suit.
The case was settled in December 1950.
In 1952 Waksman alone received the Nobel Prize, and this drew much criticism.
Schatz protested being left out of the award, and even sent a letter to the King of Sweden.
Only in the 1980s did researchers begin to credit Schatz.

Elizabeth Bugie was not given credit for her work on streptomycin and was not listed on the patent application, because she signed an affidavit stating that she had not contributed to the discovery of streptomycin.

disagreements.question: Where did the strain from which streptomycin was isolated come from?

disagreements.question: When did the first clinical trials begin?

Another text in Encyclopedia.com: the first trials in human tuberculosis began in 1945

disagreements.question: When was the Rutgers Institute of Microbiology founded?

versions.says: EBSCO: in 1949
Encyclopedia.com: in 1951 most of the royalties were assigned to its establishment

disagreements.question: How many antibiotics did Waksman and his team discover?

Another source in Encyclopedia.com: Waksman and his coworkers isolated twenty-two new defensive compounds from soil microbes

disagreements.question: What did Schatz receive in the end?

claims.text: לפי שאסטרה, שץ גידל זני סטרפטומיצס גריסאוס משני מקורות: זבל טרי ליד המעבדה ומשטח גרון מתרנגולת בריאה.
claims.quote: he began culturing strains of a bacterium called Streptomyces griseus taken from two sources: fresh manure found near the lab and a throat swab from a healthy chicken

claims.text: לפי EBSCO, בחודש אוגוסט 1943 ואקסמן ותלמידיו בודדו משני זנים של סטרפטומיצס גריסאוס חומר ששמו סטרפטומיצין.
claims.quote: The good news came in August, 1943. From two strains of streptomyces griseus, Waksman and his students isolated a substance that they dubbed streptomycin.

claims.text: לפי יומן אודסה, ואקסמן גילה את הסטרפטומיצין ב-1942.
claims.quote: In 1942, Selman discovered streptomycin, but this did not bring the scientist closer to solving the

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, מהניסויים הקליניים הראשונים ב-1944 הסטרפטומיצין הוכיח יעילות רבה נגד שחפת.
claims.quote: From the time of its first clinical trials in 1944, it proved to be remarkably effective against tuberculosis

claims.text: לפי טקסט אחר באנציקלופדיה.קום, הניסויים הקליניים הראשונים בשחפת בבני אדם החלו ב-1945.
claims.quote: The first clinical trials in human tuberculosis began in 1945.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, ואקסמן עצמו גילה שמונה עשרה אנטיביוטיקות במהלך הקריירה שלו.
claims.quote: Waksman himself discovered eighteen antibiotics during the course of his career.

claims.text: לפי מקור אחר באנציקלופדיה.קום, ואקסמן ושותפיו בודדו עשרים ושניים תרכובות הגנה חדשות מחיידקי אדמה.
claims.quote: He and coworkers isolated twenty-two new defensive compounds produced by soil microbes and in the process discovered streptomycin

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, מעבדתו של ואקסמן בודדה יותר מ-15 אנטיביוטיקות.
claims.quote: isolating more than 15 antibiotics, including streptomycin, which was the first effective treatment for tuberculosis

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, שץ קיבל 120,000 דולר עבור זכויות פטנט ו-3% מהתמלוגים.
claims.quote: Schatz was awarded $120,000 for patent rights and 3% of royalties.

claims.text: לפי וודרוף, ואקסמן הציע שהעשירית מהתמלוגים תועבר ל-26 אנשים שהיו מעורבים בסטרפטומיצין, ושץ, כמגלה, יקבל את החלק הגדול ביותר.
claims.quote: He proposed that 10% of the royalties should be passed to them, 26 persons in all

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, ואקסמן ציין ששץ היה בצבא ב-1943, שהה במעבדה רק שלושה חודשים ומילא תפקיד קטן בגילוי.
claims.quote: Waksman noted that Schatz was away at the military in 1943, adding that he was only in the lab for three months and only played a small role in discovering streptomycin.

claims.text: לפי וודרוף, סטודנטים בבית הספר לחקלאות בראטגרס התעקשו על הצבת שלט שמציין את שץ כמגלה שותף של הסטרפטומיצין, וכך נעשה.
claims.quote: Later, Rutgers Agriculture School students insisted that a plaque showing that Albert Schatz was truly a codiscoverer of streptomycin must be placed in the building

claims.text: לפי הארכיון של ספריות אוניברסיטת רוטגרס, סלמן אברהם ואקסמן נולד בפרילוקה שברוסיה ב-22 ביולי 1888.
claims.quote: Selman Abraham Waksman was born in Priluka, Russia, on July 22, 1888.
